chunks: "Because a brushless motor has no commutator.
In a brushed motor the brushes and commutator automatically switch the coil current as the rotor turns, so the torque keeps the same sign.
In a brushless motor the magnets are on the rotor and the coils are fixed, so there's nothing mechanical to do that switching.
Something electronic has to energise the right windings at the right moment, and that's what the ESC does.
If I just put DC on two of the three wires, the stator makes a fixed magnetic field.
The rotor magnet swings to line up with it, overshoots a bit, and then stops, locked in place, drawing current through a pair of windings with no back-EMF to limit it.
The motor only rotates if the stator field keeps moving ahead of the rotor, which needs the controller to know where the rotor is and step the phases in sequence.
The ESC also takes care of other things you need anyway.

It sets the speed by PWMing the voltage, it limits current so the windings and the battery are protected, it handles startup, since a sensorless motor can't see its position at standstill, and it can brake or protect against undervoltage.
The word 'often' is fair: some motors, like PC fans and hard-drive spindles, have the commutation electronics built in, so it looks like a DC motor from outside.
But the function is still there. And in industrial drives the same job is done by an inverter."
